Check: SIZE (one position)
A position cap limits what a single failure can cost. "Allowed by your rules" and "advisable" are different tests. Advertised yields vary, and a vault deposit is not an insured bank balance.
The pool, the ETH and the ten percent
Check: SIZE (cumulative)
Caps work on the whole portfolio, not one trade at a time. Check the running total before you add a second position.
The premium is due
Check: FUNDING (cash vs borrowing vs selling)

Pay known bills from cash you already have. Borrowing against crypto adds interest and a forced-sale risk, and selling adds fees and, in real life, possible tax. Use them when cash is actually short, and compare the costs.
ETH is down 40%
Check: LEVERAGE

Leverage turns a price drop into a deadline; without leverage it is only a mark-to-market loss. Compare your loan-to-value with your own line, not with the lender's. More collateral is not automatically enough.
The vote, and the permission
Check: PERMISSION

Approving a spender is a permission, not a vote. Prefer one-time signatures and exact amounts. Review and revoke approvals you no longer need. Governance power is worth using only if you have read what you are voting on.
The yield vault has been exploited
Check: PROTOCOL RISK

When a protocol is exploited, decide on what is known: how much is at risk, what has been announced, and what you can still control. Never add to a position in an unresolved incident because the price looks lower.
Rebalance day
Check: DRIFT. Two different kinds of rule apply

A purchase limit stops what you buy; a rebalancing trigger tells you when to sell back toward a total. Positions drift with prices, so check total exposure and each position, and never describe a trade as restoring a limit it did not restore.

blurb: A 31-year-old investor with a written rulebook: position caps, a borrowing line, a premium to pay, an approval trap, an exploit and a rebalancing day.
intro: Jules Park, 31, a professional who is curious about crypto and already invests. Take-home pay $3,700 a month. Living costs $2,800 a month. Opening: checking $1,200, emergency reserve $5,600, index fund $20,000, retirement account $30,000, so the investment base starts at $50,000. No DeFi (decentralized finance: crypto services run by software rather than by a bank), no debt. All figures in this scenario are assumptions for the exercise.
name: Jules Park
plan: 5% per position: no single DeFi position above 5% of the investment base.
10% in total: all DeFi positions together stay at or under 10% of the base.

Caps are tested before each purchase, against the base as it stands when he decides, counting the full purchase amount (fee included). Exactly at a cap is allowed. A position can drift above 5% as prices rise; that is not a purchase breach, but he cannot add to it.
Rebalancing trigger: 8% of the base, measured on total DeFi (yield vault + liquidity pool + ETH). ETH is Ether, the main crypto asset of the Ethereum network.
Cash for bills, not borrowing or selling, when checking already covers the bill. The $5,600 reserve is the last resort.
Investment base = index fund + retirement account + DeFi positions, at market value. Checking, the reserve and loans are not in it.
